title: India Caps Diesel Sales at 200 Litres a Day and Bars Bulk Buyers From Petrol Pumps. The Order Lasts 90 Days.
excerpt: The most sweeping fuel restrictions since the Iran war began are framed as supply management — not rationing. The government says India has two months of reserves.
body:
India has barred industrial, commercial, and institutional buyers from purchasing petrol and diesel at retail fuel stations, and capped daily diesel sales at 200 litres per vehicle — the most sweeping fuel restrictions the country has imposed since the Iran war began in February.

The Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas issued the order on June 11 under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955. It will remain in force for 90 days unless the government extends or revokes it earlier. The stated aim is to prevent "diversion, hoarding, and black marketing" of retail-priced fuel that has been underpriced relative to bulk supply channels.

## What Changed

Under the Motor Spirit and High-Speed Diesel (Temporary Regulation of Supply through Retail Outlets) Order, 2026, three restrictions now apply.

Retail outlets may sell no more than 200 litres of diesel to any single customer or vehicle in a day. The diesel must be dispensed directly into a vehicle's tank or a PESO-approved container — and it cannot be resold. Industrial and institutional users are barred from buying fuel at retail pumps altogether, and must source their requirements from their own consumer or captive pumps.

Oil marketing companies — Indian Oil, Bharat Petroleum, and Hindustan Petroleum — and their retail dealers are responsible for enforcement. State governments have been directed to act against black marketing or unauthorized diversion. Violations carry penalties under the Essential Commodities Act.

## Why Now

The government noticed a sharp spike in fuel sales at retail outlets in certain parts of the country. The reason was straightforward: retail prices, while rising, remained lower than bulk supply rates. Trucking companies, factories, and commercial operators had begun routing their purchases through retail pumps, draining supplies meant for everyday motorists.

Since mid-May, petrol prices in Delhi have climbed by ₹4.75 per litre — roughly five per cent — while diesel has risen ₹4.82 per litre, about 5.5 per cent. State-run retailers have raised pump prices four times since the start of May, each hike reflecting sustained pressure from global crude benchmarks that remain roughly 30 per cent above pre-war levels.

India, the world's third-largest oil importer and consumer, ships in about 90 per cent of its crude. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz after the U.S.-Iran war began in February disrupted a corridor that once carried a fifth of the world's oil and LNG traffic. Oil-and-gas import bills jumped 53 per cent in April alone.

## Not Rationing — Yet

The government has been careful to frame the restrictions as a supply-management tool rather than rationing. "This is not a rationing measure, and there is no shortage of petrol or diesel in the country," the order stated. Officials pointed out that India remains the world's fourth-largest refiner and fifth-largest exporter of refined petroleum products.

Sujata Sharma, Joint Secretary at the Ministry of Petroleum, said on June 11 that India has over two months of petrol and diesel reserves. She pointed to stable supplies of crude, LPG, and natural gas, and said 1.49 crore LPG cylinders had been delivered in the preceding three days alone.

But opposition parties see the restrictions as a sign of a deeper crisis. The Congress party, in a 76-page report on the Modi government's economic performance, argued that the government had benefited from years of low crude prices by raising taxes instead of passing relief to consumers — and was now shifting the burden of higher prices onto households. Senior Congress leader Rajeev Gowda urged the government to "swallow that bitter pill" rather than pass costs to consumers.

## What NRIs Should Watch

For NRIs remitting money to families in India, the cascading cost of the energy shock is hard to miss. Fuel price hikes feed into transport costs, food prices, and household budgets. The RBI now projects inflation averaging 5.1 per cent for the fiscal year ending March 2027, up from 3.48 per cent in April.

The fiscal picture is tightening in parallel. Reports indicate the government is willing to let the budget deficit widen to 4.8 per cent of GDP — half a percentage point above the 4.3 per cent target set in February — as energy subsidies and fuel costs eat into government finances. A wider deficit could slow capital expenditure, which has been the government's primary growth lever.

The 90-day window on these restrictions will expire around September — roughly in line with the deadline for the RBI's concessional forex swap facility designed to attract NRI dollar deposits. Both measures are wartime instruments. Whether they remain temporary will depend on whether the U.S.-Iran peace framework that both sides signalled on Friday actually holds.
